answer:
Azure Backup encrypts backup data at multiple levels:

**Data at rest:**
- By default, all backup data is encrypted using platform-managed keys (also called Microsoft-managed keys), with no explicit action required; data at rest is encrypted with 256-bit AES encryption that is FIPS 140-2 compliant [1][2][3][6].
- You can optionally use customer-managed keys (CMK) — RSA keys stored in Azure Key Vault that you own and manage — for greater control. The data is protected with an AES 256-based data encryption key (DEK), which is in turn protected by your keys; you must grant the vault access to the key, and you can disable or revoke access at any time [1][2][3].
- Infrastructure-level encryption can be added on top of CMK, providing two-layer (double) encryption of backup data at the storage infrastructure level; it can only be configured if you first choose your own keys, and only at vault creation time [1][2][9].
- For on-premises backups with the MARS agent, data is encrypted with a passphrase (at least 16 characters) before upload and decrypted only after download; Microsoft never decrypts backup data and doesn't keep a copy of the key [3][4][9].

**Data in transit:**
- All data in transit is transferred over HTTPS and TLS 1.2+, and remains on the Azure backbone network [1][2][3][6].

**Workload-level encryption:**
- Azure Backup supports backing up VMs with disks encrypted using platform-managed keys, customer-managed keys, or Azure Disk Encryption (BitLocker for Windows, DM-Crypt for Linux), and TDE-enabled SQL databases [1][2][3].

citations.title: Encryption in Azure Backup
citations.text:
Encryption in Azure Backup
Encryption levels

Azure Backup automatically encrypts all your backed\-up data while storing in the cloud using Azure Storage encryption, which helps you meet your security and compliance commitments. This data at rest is encrypted using 256\-bit AES encryption (one of the strongest block ciphers available that is FIPS 140\-2 compliant). Additionally, all your backup data in transit is transferred over HTTPS. It always remains on the Azure backbone network.

This article describes the levels of encryption in Azure Backup that helps to protect your backed\-up data.

Azure Backup includes encryption on two levels:

| Encryption level | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Encryption of data in the Recovery Services vault** | \- **Using platform\-managed keys**: By default, all your data is encrypted using platform\-managed keys. You don't need to take any explicit action from your end to enable this encryption. It applies to all workloads being backed\-up to your Recovery Services vault.  \- **Using customer\-managed keys**: When backing up your Azure Virtual Machines, you can choose to encrypt your data using encryption keys owned and managed by you. Azure Backup lets you use your RSA keys stored in the Azure Key Vault for encrypting your backups. The encryption key used for encrypting backups may be different from the one used for the source. The data is protected using an AES 256 based data encryption key (DEK), which is, in turn, protected using your keys. This gives you full control over the data and the keys. To allow encryption, it's required that you grant the Recovery Services vault access to the encryption key in the Azure Key Vault. You can disable the key or revoke access whenever needed. However, you must enable encryption using your keys before you attempt to protect any items to the vault. [Learn more here](encryption-at-rest-with-cmk).  \- **Infrastructure\-level encryption**: In addition to encrypting your data in the Recovery Services vault using customer\-managed keys, you can also choose to have an additional layer of encryption configured on the storage infrastructure. This infrastructure encryption is managed by the platform. Together with encryption at rest using customer\-managed keys, it allows two\-layer encryption of your backup data. Infrastructure encryption can only be configured if you first choose to use your own keys for encryption at rest. Infrastructure encryption uses platform\-managed keys for encrypting data. |
| **Encryption specific to the workload being backed\-up** | \- **Azure virtual machine backup**: Azure Backup supports backup of VMs with disks encrypted using [platform\-managed keys](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/disk-encryption#platform-managed-keys), as well as [customer\-managed keys](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/disk-encryption#customer-managed-keys) owned and managed by you. In addition, you can also back up your Azure Virtual machines that have their OS or data disks encrypted using [Azure Disk Encryption](backup-azure-vms-encryption#encryption-support-by-using-ade). ADE uses BitLocker for Windows VMs, and DM\-Crypt for Linux VMs, to perform in\-guest encryption.  \- **TDE \- enabled database backup is supported**. To restore a TDE\-encrypted database to another SQL Server, you need to first [restore the certificate to the destination server](/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/encryption/move-a-tde-protected-database-to-another-sql-server). The backup compression for TDE\-enabled databases for SQL Server 2016 and newer versions is available, but at lower transfer size as explained [here](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/sql-server/backup-compression-for-tde-enabled-databases-important-fixes-in/ba-p/385593). |

citations.title: Best practices for backup data protection
section_path: Best practices for backup data protection
Azure Backup security best practices to safeguard backup data
citations.text:
Best practices for backup data protection
Azure Backup security best practices to safeguard backup data > Pillar 2 \- Secure Backup Storage > Encryption of backup data

Encryption ensures that backup data is protected both at rest and in transit. With Azure Backup, all your backup data is encrypted by default with Microsoft\-managed keys. All the data in vaults is encrypted at rest with 256\-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) encryption compliant with Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) 140\-2\. All communication and data transfer over HTTPS and Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1\.2\+ ensuring data in transit is encrypted and remains within Azure Network. Azure Backup also supports backup and restore of Azure Virtual Machines (VMs) that have their OS/data disks encrypted with Azure Disk Encryption (ADE).

To enable control over the encryption key by configuring key rotation and lifecycle or to bring their own keys for encryption, use Customer\-Managed Keys (CMK) for encryption of the backup data. [Learn more about how to enable CMK](encryption-at-rest-with-cmk?tabs=portal&preserve-view=true).

As best practices:

* Protect CMK‑related changes with MUA by enabling Multiuser authorization on the vault. This feature prevents users with Backup Contributor permissions from changing encryption keys or the associated managed identity without approval. MUA safeguards critical operations such as switching from Microsoft‑managed keys to CMK and modifying CMK encryption settings.
* Enable infrastructure encryption at vault creation to meet compliance requirements for dual encryption at the storage layer. Infrastructure encryption applies only at creation time. You can't enable the encryption type when the datasource backup copies get stored in the vault.

[Learn more about encryption of backup data](backup-encryption).

Private endpoints for backup data transfer
Private endpoints provide secure, private connectivity to backup storage and keep data transfer within a protected network boundary. Each private endpoint uses one or more private IP addresses from your Azure Virtual Network (VNet), which brings the backup service directly into your VNet. This approach minimizes exposure to the public internet and reduces the risk of unauthorized access or data breaches. [Learn more about private endpoints for Azure Backup](backup-azure-private-endpoints-concept).

For Azure VMs, all communication and data transfer occur through the Azure fabric, so no firewall exceptions are required. For databases running on Azure VMs and for on‑premises servers, private endpoints enable secure network connectivity for backup and restore operations.

[Learn how to create and manage private endpoints (with v2 experience) for Azure Backup](backup-azure-private-endpoints-configure-manage).

citations.title: Overview
section_path: Overview of security features in Azure Backup
citations.text:
Overview
Overview of security features in Azure Backup > Encryption of data

Encryption protects your data and helps you to meet your organizational security and compliance commitments. Data encryption occurs in many stages in Azure Backup:

* Within Azure, data in transit between Azure storage and the vault is [protected by HTTPS](backup-support-matrix#network-traffic-to-azure). This data remains on the Azure backbone network.
* Backup data is automatically encrypted using [platform\-managed keys](backup-encryption), and you don't need to take any explicit action to enable it. You can also encrypt your backed\-up data using [customer managed keys](encryption-at-rest-with-cmk) stored in the Azure Key Vault. It applies to all workloads being backed up to your Recovery Services vault.
* Azure Backup supports backup and restore of Azure VMs that have their OS/data disks encrypted with [Azure Disk Encryption (ADE)](backup-azure-vms-encryption#encryption-support-by-using-ade) and [VMs with CMK encrypted disks](backup-azure-vms-encryption#encryption-by-using-customer-managed-keys). For more information, [learn more about encrypted Azure VMs and Azure Backup](backup-azure-vms-encryption).
* When data is backed up from on\-premises servers with the MARS agent, data is encrypted with a passphrase before upload to Azure Backup and decrypted only after it's downloaded from Azure Backup. Read more about [security features to help protect hybrid backups](#security-features-to-help-protect-hybrid-backups).

Soft delete
Azure Backup provides security features to help protect the backup data even after deletion. With soft delete, if you delete the backup of a VM, the backup data is retained for *14 additional days*, allowing the recovery of that backup item with no data loss. The additional *14 days retention of backup data in the "soft delete state* doesn't incur any cost. [Learn more about soft delete](backup-azure-security-feature-cloud).

Azure Backup has now also enhanced soft delete to further improve chances of recovering data after deletion. [Learn more](#enhanced-soft-delete).

Immutable vaults
Immutable vault can help you protect your backup data by blocking any operations that could lead to loss of recovery points. Further, you can lock the immutable vault setting to make it irreversible that can prevent any malicious actors from disabling immutability and deleting backups. [Learn more about immutable vaults](backup-azure-immutable-vault-concept).

Multi\-user authorization
Multi\-user authorization (MUA) for Azure Backup allows you to add an additional layer of protection to critical operations on your Recovery Services vaults and Backup vaults. For MUA, Azure Backup uses another Azure resource called the Resource Guard to ensure critical operations are performed only with applicable authorization. [Learn more about multi\-user authorization for Azure Backup](multi-user-authorization-concept).

Cross\-tenant restore (preview)
Cross\-tenant restore lets you restore vaulted backup data from a source tenant to a different target tenant after you map the source and target vaults. Use it to recover from scenarios such as tenant lockout, ransomware attacks, and tenant consolidation. Resource Guard protects the mapping operation. [Learn more about cross\-tenant restore](cross-tenant-restore-overview).

Enhanced soft delete
Enhanced soft delete provides you with the ability to recover your data even after it's deleted, accidentally or maliciously. It works by delaying the permanent deletion of data by a specified duration, providing you with an opportunity to retrieve it. You can also make soft delete *always\-on* to prevent it from being disabled. [Learn more about enhanced soft delete for Backup](backup-azure-enhanced-soft-delete-about).

Monitoring and alerts of suspicious activity
Azure Backup provides [built\-in monitoring and alerting capabilities](backup-azure-monitoring-built-in-monitor) to view and configure actions for events related to Azure Backup. [Backup Reports](configure-reports) serve as a one\-stop destination for tracking usage, auditing of backups and restores, and identifying key trends at different levels of granularity. Using Azure Backup's monitoring and reporting tools can alert you to any unauthorized, suspicious, or malicious activity as soon as they occur.

citations.title: Azure Backup architecture
citations.text:
Azure Backup architecture
Azure Backup architecture and components > Data isolation with Azure Backup

With Azure Backup, the vaulted backup data is stored in Microsoft\-managed Azure subscription and tenant. External users or guests have no direct access to this backup storage or its contents, ensuring the isolation of backup data from the production environment where the data source resides.

In Azure, all communications and data in transit is securely transferred with *HTTPS* and *TLS 1\.2\+* protocols. This data remains on the Azure backbone network ensuring reliable and efficient data transmission. The backup data at rest is encrypted by default using *Microsoft\-managed keys*. You can also bring your own keys for encryption if you require greater control over the data. To enhance protection, you can use [immutability](backup-azure-immutable-vault-concept), which prevents data from being altered or deleted before its retention period. Azure Backup gives you diverse options such as [soft delete](backup-azure-enhanced-soft-delete-about), stop backup and delete data or retain data if you need to stop backups at any time. To protect critical operations, you can add [Multi\-User Authorization (MUA)](multi-user-authorization-concept) that adds additional layer of protection by using an Azure resource called Azure Resource Guard.

This robust approach ensures that even in a compromised environment, existing backups cannot be tampered with or deleted by unauthorized users.

Learn more about vaulted backup for the following datasources:

* [Azure Files](azure-file-share-backup-overview?tabs=vault-standard#architecture-for-azure-files-backup)
* [Azure Blob](blob-backup-overview?tabs=vaulted-backup#how-the-azure-blobs-backup-works)
* [Azure Data Lake Storage](azure-data-lake-storage-backup-overview), [Azure Kubernetes](azure-kubernetes-service-backup-overview#which-backup-storage-tier-does-aks-backup-support)
* [PostgreSQL \- Flexible server](tutorial-create-first-backup-azure-database-postgresql-flex)
* [PostgreSQL database](backup-azure-database-postgresql-overview#changes-to-vaulted-backups-for-postgresql-single-servers)

section_path: Frequently asked questions \- Protect backups from Ransomware
What are the best practices to configure and protect Azure Backups against security and ransomware threats?
citations.text:
FAQ-Protection against Ransomware
Frequently asked questions \- Protect backups from Ransomware > What are the best practices to configure and protect Azure Backups against security and ransomware threats?

	+ For Azure VM, [data in transit remains on the Azure backbone network without needing to access your virtual network](security-overview#internet-connectivity-not-required-for-azure-vm-backup). Therefore, backup of Azure VMs placed inside secured networks doesn't require you to allow access to any IPs or FQDNs.
	+ For databases on Azure VM, secure the outbound access with the following network connectivity requirements [for SQL Server](backup-sql-server-database-azure-vms#establish-network-connectivity), [for SAP HANA database](backup-azure-sap-hana-database#establish-network-connectivity) on Azure VM.
	+ For PaaS resources, such as PostgreSQL, communication happens within the Azure network. For workloads (such as Azure Files, Azure Disk, and Azure Blobs) where the backup data is stored in the operational tier, you need to *allow Azure services on the trusted services list to access storage account* in *Network Settings* for the corresponding storage account.
	+ For on\-premises workloads that are protected using MARS or MABS, can use Microsoft peering for *ExpressRoute* or *Virtual Private Network (VPN)* to connect to Azure. Use *private peering* when using *private endpoints* for Backup. Network traffic between peered virtual networks remains private.For more information, see:

	+ [Connect private networks together](/en-us/security/benchmark/azure/baselines/backup-security-baseline?toc=/azure/backup/toc.json#ns-2-connect-private-networks-together).
	+ [Establish private network access to Azure services](/en-us/security/benchmark/azure/baselines/backup-security-baseline?toc=/azure/backup/toc.json#ns-3-establish-private-network-access-to-azure-services).
	+ [Use Azure Virtual Network service tags to define network access controls for Backup resources on network security groups (NSGs) or Azure Firewall](/en-us/security/benchmark/azure/baselines/backup-security-baseline?toc=/azure/backup/toc.json#ns-6-simplify-network-security-rules).
	+ [Security features for hybrid backups that use Azure Backup](backup-azure-security-feature).
* **Ensure backup data is encrypted**.

By default, backup data at rest is encrypted using platform\-managed keys (PMK). For vaulted backups, you can choose to use customer\-managed keys (CMK) to own and manage the encryption keys yourself. Additionally, you can configure encryption on the storage infrastructure using infrastructure\-level encryption, which along with CMK encryption provides double encryption of data at rest.

	+ MARS or MABS backup allows you to use your own passphrase to allow end\-to\-end encryption of data. However, ensure that the associated *encryption passphrase* is securely stored in an alternate location (other than the source machine), preferably in the Azure Key Vault. Keep track of all the passphrases, if you've multiple machines being backed\-up with the MARS agents.
	+ You can also back up encrypted Azure VMs (encrypted using Azure Disk Encryption) and encrypted SQL Servers running in Azure VMs (encrypted using TDE) to ensure end\-to\-end encryption.For more information, see:

	+ [Encryption of data in the Recovery Services vault using CMK, PMK, Infrastructure\-level encryption](backup-encryption#encryption-levels).
	+ [Azure Storage encryption for data at rest](../storage/common/storage-service-encryption).
	+ [Transport Layer Security in Azure Backup](transport-layer-security).
* **Regularly monitor your backups**

Use the monitoring solutions (for example, Backup Explorer) to identify machines in the organization that aren’t protected by Azure Backup, monitor your backup items, backup jobs, and policies. For more information, see:

	+ [Monitoring and reporting scenarios](monitoring-and-alerts-overview).
	+ [Monitor your backups with Backup Explorer](monitor-azure-backup-with-backup-explorer).
	+ [Monitor backup workloads using Azure portal (using Recovery Services vault)](backup-azure-monitoring-built-in-monitor).
	+ [Monitor backup health using Azure monitor metrics](backup-azure-monitoring-built-in-monitor).
	+ [Custom monitoring and alerting using Azure monitor Log Analytics workspace](backup-azure-monitoring-use-azuremonitor).
* **Validate backups periodically by performing test restores**.

Periodically perform data recovery test of your backups to verify the backup configurations and availability of the backup data meet your organization’s recovery needs, and expected RPO and RTO requirements. Define your backup recovery test strategy to include the scope of test recovery and frequency for performing a test recovery.

citations.title: FAQ- Recovery Services vault
section_path: Is the data sent to Azure encrypted?
citations.text:
FAQ- Recovery Services vault
Azure Backup \- Frequently asked questions > Encryption > Is the data sent to Azure encrypted?

Yes. Data is encrypted on the on\-premises machine using AES256\. The data is sent over a secure HTTPS link. The data transmitted in cloud is protected by HTTPS link only between storage and recovery service. iSCSI protocol secures the data transmitted between recovery service and user machine. Secure tunneling is used to protect the iSCSI channel.

Is the backup data on Azure encrypted as well?
Yes. The data in Azure is encrypted\-at\-rest.

* For on\-premises backup, encryption\-at\-rest is provided using the passphrase you provide when backing up to Azure.
* For Azure VMs, data is encrypted\-at\-rest using Storage Service Encryption (SSE).

Microsoft doesn't decrypt the backup data at any point.

What is the minimum length of the encryption key used to encrypt backup data?
The encryption key used by the Microsoft Azure Recovery Services (MARS) Agent is derived from a passphrase that should be at least 16 characters long. For Azure VMs, there's no limit to the length of keys used by Azure KeyVault.

What happens if I misplace the encryption key? Can I recover the data? Can Microsoft recover the data?
The key used to encrypt the backup data is present only on your site. Microsoft doesn't maintain a copy in Azure and doesn't have any access to the key. If you misplace the key, Microsoft can't recover the backup data.

Amazon Redshift clusters can be backed up with AWS Backup [4][9]. The AWS Backup console provides two ways to back up a cluster: on demand or as part of a backup plan [1]. When clusters are included as protected resources in a backup plan, AWS Backup provides scheduled backups [2]. The AWS Backup console [3] and AWS CLI [7] can be used to back up clusters.

AWS Backup provides automated snapshot capability for Amazon Redshift clusters, with a retention period of 0 to 35 days [5], and supports cloud-native backups of Amazon Redshift clusters [6]. AWS Backup also provides immutable backups for Amazon Redshift data warehouses [12]. Additionally, AWS Backup supports backing up Amazon Redshift Serverless [15].

answer:
## Configuring Cross Region Restore

**Recovery Services vault:**
1. In the Azure portal, go to your Recovery Services vault, and under **Settings**, select **Properties** [2][3].
2. Under **Backup Configuration**, select **Update** [2][3].
3. Under **Cross Region Restore**, select **Enable** [2][3].

**Backup vault (e.g., for PostgreSQL):**
1. Sign in to the Azure portal [1][4].
2. Create a new Backup vault or choose an existing one, then go to **Properties** (or **Manage** > **Properties**) and under **Vault Settings**, select **Update** next to **Cross Region Restore**, then choose **Enable** [1][4].

**Prerequisites and considerations:**
- Cross Region Restore is supported only for a vault that uses Geo-redundant (GRS) storage redundancy [2][3][4].
- It incurs extra charges, and after enabling, it may take up to 48 hours for backup items to be available in secondary regions [2][3][4].
- Once protection starts, Cross Region Restore can't be reverted to GRS or LRS [2][3].
- Permissions (Azure RBAC) are required to use Cross Region Restore [2][3].
- If you can't view the settings despite access to restricted paired regions, re-register the Microsoft.RecoveryServices resource provider [2][3].

## Running a Cross Region Restore

**For PostgreSQL (Backup vault):**
1. After backup completes in the primary region, it can take up to 12 hours for recovery points to replicate to the secondary region [1].
2. Check availability of recovery points in the secondary region via **Backup vault** > **Backup Instances**, filtering **Instance Region** as *Secondary Region* [1].
3. Select **Restore to secondary region**, review the target region, and select the appropriate recovery point and restore parameters [1].
4. Monitor the restore under **Backup Jobs**, filtering by workload type and *Secondary Region* [1].

**For Azure VMs:**
- The secondary region restore experience is similar to the primary region; you provide only secondary region parameters in the Restore Configuration pane [5].
- Cross Region Restore supports the **Create a VM** and **Restore disks** options; the **Replace existing disks** option isn't supported [6][7].
- Only vault-tier data is replicated (snapshots aren't), so secondary region restores are vault-tier restores only [6].
- For restoring disks via template, the **Staging Location** (storage account) must be in the vault's secondary region [5].
- Backup admins and app admins have permissions to perform the restore operation in the secondary region [6][7].
- Cross-region restore can also be automated via PowerShell, CLI, and REST API [10].

citations.title: Create
section_path: Create and configure a Recovery Services vault
citations.text:
Create
Create and configure a Recovery Services vault > Set Cross Region Restore

With the Cross Region Restore option, you can restore data in a secondary, [Azure paired region](/en-us/azure/reliability/cross-region-replication-azure). You can use Cross Region Restore to conduct drills when there's an audit or compliance requirement. You can also use it to restore the data if there's a disaster in the primary region.

Before you begin, consider the following information:

* Cross Region Restore is supported only for a Recovery Services vault that uses the [GRS replication type](#set-storage-redundancy).
* Virtual machines (VMs) created through Azure Resource Manager and encrypted Azure VMs are supported. VMs created through the classic deployment model aren't supported. You can restore the VM or its disk.
* SQL Server or SAP HANA databases hosted on Azure VMs are supported. You can restore databases or their files.
* The Recovery Services agent is supported for vaults without a private endpoint (preview).
* A list of supported managed types and regions is available in the [Support matrix for Azure Backup](backup-support-matrix#cross-region-restore).
* Cross Region Restore incurs extra charges for use. After you enable Cross Region Restore, it might take up to 48 hours for the backup items to be available in secondary regions. [Learn more about pricing](https://azure.microsoft.com/pricing/details/backup/).
* Cross Region Restore currently can't be reverted to GRS or LRS after the protection starts for the first time.
* Secondary region recovery point objective (RPO) can vary by workload type and policy. For Azure VM backups, the secondary region RPO can be up to 36 hours in the worst case. With the Standard policy, the primary region RPO is up to 24 hours, and replication to the secondary region can take up to 12 hours. With the Enhanced policy, more frequent local recovery point creation can improve the best\-case achievable secondary region RPO, but the worst\-case can still be up to 36 hours. For workload\-specific guidance, see the relevant restore documentation.
* Permissions are required to use Cross Region Restore. For more information, see [Use Azure role\-based access control (RBAC) to manage Azure Backup recovery points](backup-rbac-rs-vault#minimum-role-requirements-for-azure-vm-backup).

A vault created with GRS redundancy includes the option to configure Cross Region Restore. Every GRS vault has a banner that links to the documentation.

Cross Region Restore is also supported for machines running on Ultra Disks. [Learn more about Ultra Disk backup supportability](backup-support-matrix-iaas#ultra-disk-backup).

![Screenshot that shows the banner about backup configuration.](/media/55f4325b-713c-4453-8a90-5d3f6a163718/02179986be29.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the Recovery Services vault overview page showing a banner about the cross-region restore feature and sections for Backup and Site Recovery with quick links.

To configure Cross Region Restore for the vault:

1. From the Azure portal, go to your Recovery Services vault, and then under **Settings**, select **Properties**.
2. Under **Backup Configuration**, select **Update**.
3. Under **Cross Region Restore**, select **Enable**.

![Screenshot that shows the Backup Configuration pane and the toggle for enabling Cross Region Restore.](/media/55f4325b-713c-4453-8a90-5d3f6a163718/dd2e2c39fc39.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the Backup Configuration pane showing the Storage replication type options (Locally-redundant and Geo-redundant) and the Cross Region Restore toggle with Enable and Disable buttons. The Cross Region Restore feature is currently disabled, and a note explains it allows restoration in the secondary region for BCDR drills and outages.

Note

If you have access to restricted paired regions and still can't view Cross Region Restore settings on the **Backup Configuration** pane, re\-register the Recovery Services resource provider. To re\-register the provider, go to your subscription in the Azure portal, go to **Resource provider** on the left pane, and then select **Microsoft.RecoveryServices** \> **Re\-register**.

For more information about backup and restore with Cross Region Restore, see these articles:

* [Cross Region Restore for Azure VMs](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#cross-region-restore)
* [Cross Region Restore for SQL Server databases](restore-sql-database-azure-vm#cross-region-restore)
* [Cross Region Restore for SAP HANA databases](sap-hana-db-restore#cross-region-restore)
* [Cross Region Restore for MARS (preview)](about-restore-microsoft-azure-recovery-services#cross-region-restore-for-mars)

* [Cross Region Restore for Azure VMs](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#cross-region-restore)
* [Cross Region Restore for SQL Server databases](restore-sql-database-azure-vm#cross-region-restore)
* [Cross Region Restore for SAP HANA databases](sap-hana-db-restore#cross-region-restore)
* [Cross Region Restore for MARS (preview)](about-restore-microsoft-azure-recovery-services#cross-region-restore-for-mars)

Manage
Manage Backup vaults > Perform Cross Region Restore using Azure portal

The Cross Region Restore option allows you to restore data in a secondary Azure paired region. To configure Cross Region Restore for the backup vault: 

1. Sign in to [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com/).
2. [Create a new Backup vault](create-manage-backup-vault#create-backup-vault) or choose an existing Backup vault, and then enable Cross Region Restore by going to **Properties** \> **Cross Region Restore**, and choose **Enable**.

[

![Screenshot shows how to enable Cross Region Restore for PostgreSQL database.](/media/bf5b97e5-55ca-4136-9bbc-1dcf7da6221d/5f0ccd8153d4.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the Azure Backup vault properties page showing the 'Cross Region Restore (Preview)' setting as 'Enabled' in the Vault Settings section, with a separate 'Cross Region Restore' dialog open on the right, displaying an 'Enable' toggle and notes about the feature's requirements and impact.

](media/backup-vault-overview/enable-cross-region-restore-for-postgresql-database.png#lightbox)
3. Go to the Backup vault’s **Overview** pane, and then [configure a backup for PostgreSQL database](backup-azure-database-postgresql).
4. Once the backup is complete in the primary region, it can take up to *12 hours* for the recovery point in the primary region to get replicated to the secondary region.

To check the availability of recovery point in the secondary region, go to the **Backup vault** \> **Backup Instances** \> **Filter to Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers**, filter **Instance Region** as *Secondary Region*, and then select the required Backup Instance.

[

![Screenshot shows how to check availability for the recovery points in the secondary region.](/media/bf5b97e5-55ca-4136-9bbc-1dcf7da6221d/091bc87fe4aa.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the 'Backup instances' page in Azure Backup, showing filters applied to view recovery points in the Secondary Region for Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers, with a list of protected instances displayed below.

](media/backup-vault-overview/check-availability-of-recovery-point-in-secondary-region.png#lightbox)

The recovery points available in the secondary region are now listed.
5. Select **Restore to secondary region**.

[

![Screenshot shows how to initiate restores to the secondary region.](/media/bf5b97e5-55ca-4136-9bbc-1dcf7da6221d/b32fef35ad9f.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the Azure Backup instance details page for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL server, showing the 'Restore to secondary region' button and a table of restore points from the secondary region (eastus2euap), including creation time, backup type, data store, and expiry time.

](media/backup-vault-overview/initiate-restore-to-secondary-region.png#lightbox)

You can also trigger restores from the respective backup instance.

[

![Screenshot shows how to trigger restores from the respective backup instance.](/media/bf5b97e5-55ca-4136-9bbc-1dcf7da6221d/edfec16bdff8.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the 'Backup instances' page in Azure Backup, showing a list of backup instances with filters applied. The context menu for a backup instance is open, highlighting the 'Restore to secondary region' option, indicating the action to trigger a restore from the backup instance.

](media/backup-vault-overview/trigger-restores-from-respective-backup-instance.png#lightbox)
6. Select **Restore to secondary region** to review the target region selected, and then select the appropriate recovery point and restore parameters.
7. Once the restore starts, you can monitor the completion of the restore operation under **Backup Jobs** of the Backup vault by filtering **Jobs workload type** to *Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers* and **Instance Region** to *Secondary Region*.

[

![Screenshot shows how to monitor the postgresql restore to the secondary region.](/media/bf5b97e5-55ca-4136-9bbc-1dcf7da6221d/d5cfce9d2d2f.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the 'Backup jobs' page in an Azure Backup vault, showing completed CrossRegionRestore operations for Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers in the Secondary Region. Filters are applied for 'Datasource type' and 'Instance Region' to display relevant restore jobs.

](media/backup-vault-overview/monitor-postgresql-restore-to-secondary-region.png#lightbox)

Note

Cross Region Restore is currently only available for PostgreSQL servers.

citations.text:
Restore
Tutorial: Restore Azure Database for PostgreSQL \- Flexible Server using Azure portal > Prerequisites

Tutorial: Restore Azure Database for PostgreSQL \- Flexible Server using Azure portal
This tutorial describes how to restore Azure Database for PostgreSQL \- Flexible Server using the Azure portal.

Before you restore Azure Database for PostgreSQL \- Flexible Server, ensure the following prerequisites are met:

* Cross Region Restore is supported only for a Backup vault that uses **Storage Redundancy** as **Geo\-redundant**.
* Review the [support matrix](backup-azure-database-postgresql-flex-support-matrix) for a list of supported managed types and regions.
* Cross Region Restore incurs extra charges. Learn more about [pricing](https://azure.microsoft.com/pricing/details/backup/).
* Once you enable Cross Region Restore, it might take up to **48 hours** for the backup items to be available in secondary regions.
* Review the [permissions required to use Cross Region Restore](backup-rbac-rs-vault#minimum-role-requirements-for-azure-vm-backup).

Note

A vault created with **Geo\-redundant storage** option enabled allows you to configure the **Cross Region Restore** feature. The Cross Region Restore feature allows you to restore data in a secondary [Azure paired region](/en-us/azure/availability-zones/cross-region-replication-azure) even when no outage occurs in the primary region; thus, enabling you to perform drills to assess regional resiliency. 

Enable Immutability in Backup vault
Immutability in Azure Backup vault is a feature designed to protect your backup data by preventing any operations that could lead to the loss of recovery points. This feature ensures that once data is written to the vault, it can't be modified or deleted, even by administrators.

To enable immutability in the Backup vault, follow these steps:

1. Sign in to the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com/)
2. [Create a new Backup vault](create-manage-backup-vault#create-backup-vault) or choose an existing Backup vault.
3. [Enable vault immutability](backup-azure-immutable-vault-how-to-manage?tabs=backup-vault#enable-immutable-vault).

Enable Cross Region Restore in Backup vault
Cross Region Restore allows you to restore data in a secondary Azure paired region.

To configure Cross Region Restore for the backup vault, follow these steps:

1. Sign in to the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com/).
2. Go to the **Backup vault** you created, and then select **Manage** \> **Properties**.
3. Under **Vault Settings**, select **Update** corresponding to **Cross Region Restore**.
4. Under **Cross Region Restore**, select **Enable**.

[

![Screenshot shows how to enable Cross Region Restore in the Backup vault.](/media/e53dfaee-916c-4947-9224-43ba63f6a14f/e2f9809afce1.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the Backup vault properties page showing the 'Cross Region Restore' setting as 'Disabled' with an 'Update' link, and a modal dialog explaining the feature and its requirements.

](media/tutorial-restore-postgresql-flex/enable-cross-region-restore.png#lightbox)

View backup instances in secondary region
If Cross Region Restore is enabled, you can view the backup instances in the secondary region.

To view the backup instances, follow these steps:

1. In the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com/), go to your **Backup vault**.
2. Under **Manage**, select **Backup instances**.
3. Select **Instance Region \=\= Secondary Region** on the filters.

[

![Screenshot shows how to view the protected instance of a database.](/media/e53dfaee-916c-4947-9224-43ba63f6a14f/af48319cfc50.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the 'Backup instances' page in Azure Backup vault, showing a list of protected database instances with filters applied, including 'Instance Region = Secondary Region'. The table displays one instance named 'pgflex-demo' with protection status 'Protection configured'.

](media/tutorial-restore-postgresql-flex/view-database-backup-instance.png#lightbox)

citations.title: Restore Azure VMs in the portal
section_path: Restore Azure VMs in the portal
How to restore Azure VM data in Azure portal
citations.text:
Restore Azure VMs in the portal
How to restore Azure VM data in Azure portal > Cross Region Restore > Restore in secondary region

The secondary region restore user experience is similar to the primary region restore user experience. When configuring details in the Restore Configuration pane to configure your restore, you're prompted to provide only secondary region parameters.

For Azure VM backups, the secondary region [RPO](azure-backup-glossary#recovery-point-objective-rpo) can be up to *36 hours* in the worst case. With the Standard policy, the primary region RPO is up to *24 hours*, and replication to the secondary region can take up to *12 hours*. With the Enhanced policy, more frequent local recovery point creation can improve the best\-case achievable secondary region RPO. However, because vaulting is daily, the worst\-case secondary region RPO can still be up to *36 hours*.

![{alt-text}](/media/abf6cef2-67dc-48d8-ba60-bacc79bfcdb4/be7651d7cd5bd8d2.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the 'Recover' page in a resilience management interface, showing fields for resource environment, datasource type, and recovery details. The 'Recovery action' dropdown is highlighted, set to 'Restore to secondary region', with 'Azure Virtual machines' and 'Azure Backup' selected as datasource type and solution respectively.

Screenshot shows how to start secondary region restore of a VM. ":::

![Screenshot shows a restore point is selected for secondary region restore.](/media/abf6cef2-67dc-48d8-ba60-bacc79bfcdb4/7132025adeec0a8f.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the 'Restore Virtual Machine' dialog in a resiliency tool, showing a selected restore point (7/27/2025, 7:58:03 AM) for a secondary region restore. The form includes fields for restore target, restore type, virtual machine name, subscription, resource group, virtual network, subnet, and staging location, with the 'Restore' button at the bottom.

* To restore and create a VM, refer to [Create a VM](#create-a-vm).
* To restore as a disk, refer to [Restore disks](#restore-disks).

Note

* The Cross Region Restore feature restores CMK (customer\-managed keys) enabled Azure VMs, which aren't backed\-up in a CMK enabled Recovery Services vault, as non\-CMK enabled VMs in the secondary region.
* The Azure roles needed to restore in the secondary region are the same as those in the primary region.
* When you restore an Azure VM, Azure Backup configures the virtual network settings in the secondary region automatically. If you are [restoring disks](#restore-disks) while deploying the template, ensure to provide the virtual network settings, corresponding to the secondary region.
* If VNet/Subnet is not available in the primary region or is not configured in the secondary region, Azure portal doesn't auto\-populate any default values during restore operation.
* For Cross Region Restores, the **Staging Location** (that is the storage account location) must be in the region that the Recovery Services vault treats as the *secondary* region. For example, a Recovery Services vault is located in East US 2 region (with Geo\-Redundancy and Cross Region Restore enabled). This means that the *secondary* region would be *Central US*. Therefore, you need to create a storage account in *Central US* to perform a Cross Region Restore of the VM.   
 Learn more about [Azure cross\-region replication pairings for all geographies](/en-us/azure/reliability/cross-region-replication-azure).

[Azure zone pinned VMs](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/create-portal-availability-zone) can be restored in any [availability zones](/en-us/azure/reliability/availability-zones-overview) of the same region.

In the restore process, you'll see the option **Availability Zone.** You'll see your default zone first. To choose a different zone, choose the number of the zone of your choice. If the pinned zone is unavailable, you won't be able to restore the data to another zone because the backed\-up data isn't replicated across zones. The restore in availability zones is possible from recovery points in vault tier only.

In summary, the **Availability Zone** will only appear when

* The source VM is zone pinned and is NOT encrypted
* The recovery point is present in vault tier (Snapshots only are not supported)
* The recovery option is to either create a new VM or to restore disks (replace disks option replaces source data and hence the availability zone option is not applicable)
* Creating VM/disks in the same region when vault's storage redundancy is ZRS (Doesn't work when vault's storage redundancy is GRS even though the source VM is zone pinned)
* Creating VM/disks in the paired region when vault's storage redundancy is enabled for Cross\-Region\-Restore AND if the paired region supports zones

citations.title: Restore Azure VMs in the portal
section_path: Restore Azure VMs in the portal
How to restore Azure VM data in Azure portal
citations.text:
Restore Azure VMs in the portal
How to restore Azure VM data in Azure portal > Restore options

| **Restore option** | **Details** |
| --- | --- |
| **Create a new VM** | Quickly creates and gets a basic VM up and running from a restore point. You can specify a name for the VM and select the resource group and virtual network (VNet) in which it will be placed. The new VM must be created in the same region as the source VM.If a VM restore fails because an Azure VM SKU wasn't available in the specified region of Azure, or because of any other issues, Azure Backup still restores the disks in the specified resource group. |
| **Restore disk** | Restores a VM disk, which can then be used to create a new VM. Azure Backup provides a template to help you customize and create a VM.  The restore job generates a template that you can download and use to specify custom VM settings, and create a VM. The disks are copied to the Resource Group you specify. Alternatively, you can attach the disk to an existing VM, or create a new VM using PowerShell. This option is useful if you want to customize the VM, add configuration settings that weren't there at the time of backup, or add settings that must be configured using the template or PowerShell. |
| **Replace existing** | You can restore a disk, and use it to replace a disk on the existing VM. The current VM must exist. If it's been deleted, this option can't be used. Azure Backup takes a snapshot of the existing VM before replacing the disk. The snapshot is copied to the vault and retained in accordance with the retention policy.　 When you choose a Vault\-Standard recovery point, a VHD file with the content of the chosen recovery point is also created in the staging location you specify. Existing disks connected to the VM are replaced with the selected restore point.  After the disk replacement operation is complete, the original disk is retained in the resource group. You can choose to manually delete the original disks if they aren't needed. Replace existing is supported for unencrypted managed VMs, including VMs [created using custom images](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/tutorial-custom-images). It's unsupported for classic VMs, unmanaged VMs, and [generalized VMs](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/upload-generalized-managed). If the restore point has more or less disks than the current VM, then the number of disks in the restore point will only reflect the VM configuration. Replace existing is also supported for VMs with linked resources, like [user\-assigned managed\-identity](../active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview) or [Key Vault](/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/overview). |
| **Cross Region (secondary region)** | Cross Region restore can be used to restore Azure VMs in the secondary region, which is an [Azure paired region](../availability-zones/cross-region-replication-azure). You can restore all the Azure VMs for the selected recovery point if the backup is done in the secondary region. During the backup, snapshots aren't replicated to the secondary region. Only the data stored in the vault is replicated. So secondary region restores are only [vault tier](about-azure-vm-restore#key-concepts-for-azure-vm-restore) restores. The restore time for the secondary region will be almost the same as the vault tier restore time for the primary region.  This feature is available for the options below: \- [Create a VM](#create-a-vm)  \- [Restore Disks](#restore-disks)  If the source machine has more than 16 disks, VHDs won't be created in Cross Region Restore.  We don't currently support the [Replace existing disks](#replace-existing-disks) option. Permissions The restore operation on secondary region can be performed by Backup Admins and App admins. |
| **Cross Subscription Restore** | Allows you to restore managed Azure virtual machines or disks to a different subscription within the same tenant as the protected VM, subject to Azure RBAC permissions.  The default target subscription is the protected VM subscription. Cross Subscription Restore works with [Cross Region Restore](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#cross-region-restore) and [Cross Zonal Restore](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#create-a-vm).  Supported behavior depends on the recovery point tier: \- Snapshot\-tier recovery points can be restored only in the protected VM subscription.  \- Vault\-tier recovery points can be restored in the protected VM subscription or the vault subscription. To restore a vault\-tier recovery point to another subscription, the [Cross Subscription Restore property](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#cross-subscription-restore-for-azure-vm) must be enabled on the Recovery Services vault.  Original location restore and [Replace existing disk](#replace-existing-disks) are supported only in the protected VM subscription. Cross Subscription Restore is supported for [Restore with Managed System Identities (MSI)](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#restore-vms-with-managed-identities).  It's unsupported for legacy recovery points from [VMs that used unmanaged disks](#restore-legacy-recovery-points-from-vms-that-used-unmanaged-disks), [ADE encrypted VMs](backup-azure-vms-encryption#encryption-support-by-using-ade), and [VMs with CMK encrypted disks](backup-azure-vms-encryption). |
| **Cross Tenant Restore (preview)** | You can restore vaulted recovery points of managed Azure virtual machines to a different tenant after you map the source and target Recovery Services vaults.  Only alternate location restore is supported. Snapshot\-tier recovery points, original location restore, Confidential VMs, VMs encrypted with Azure Disk Encryption (ADE), and archive\-tier recovery points aren't supported.  [Learn more about cross\-tenant restore](cross-tenant-restore-overview). |
| **Cross Zonal Restore** | Allows you to restore Azure Virtual Machines or disks pinned to any zone to different available zones (as per the Azure RBAC capabilities) from restore points. Note that when you select a zone to restore, it selects the [logical zone](/en-us/azure/reliability/availability-zones-overview#zonal-and-zone-redundant-services) (and not the physical zone) as per the Azure subscription you will use to restore to.  You can trigger Cross Zonal Restore for managed virtual machines only.  Cross Zonal Restore is supported for [Restore with Managed System Identities (MSI)](#restore-vms-with-managed-identities).  Cross Zonal Restore supports restore of an Azure zone pinned/non\-zone pinned VM from a vault with Zonal\-redundant storage (ZRS) enabled. Learn [how to set Storage Redundancy](backup-create-rs-vault#set-storage-redundancy).  It's supported to restore an Azure zone pinned VM only from a [vault with Cross Region Restore (CRR)](backup-create-rs-vault#set-storage-redundancy) (if the secondary region supports zones) or Zone Redundant Storage (ZRS) enabled.  Cross Zonal Restore is supported from [secondary regions](#restore-in-secondary-region).  It's unsupported from [snapshots](backup-azure-vms-introduction#snapshot-creation) restore point.  It's unsupported for [Encrypted Azure VMs](backup-azure-vms-introduction#encryption-of-azure-vm-backups). |

section_path: Support matrix for Azure VM backups
citations.text:
Support matrix
Support matrix for Azure VM backups > Supported restore methods

| **Restore option** | **Details** |
| --- | --- |
| **Create a new VM** | This option quickly creates and gets a basic VM up and running from a restore point. You can specify a name for the VM, select the resource group and virtual network in which it will be placed, and specify a storage account for the restored VM. The new VM must be created in the same region as the source VM. |
| **Restore disk** | This option restores a VM disk, which can you can then use to create a new VM. Azure Backup provides a template to help you customize and create a VM.  The restore job generates a template that you can download and use to specify custom VM settings and create a VM. The disks are copied to the resource group that you specify. Alternatively, you can attach the disk to an existing VM, or create a new VM by using PowerShell. This option is useful if you want to customize the VM, add configuration settings that weren't there at the time of backup, or add settings that must be configured via the template or PowerShell. |
| **Replace existing** | You can restore a disk and use it to replace a disk on the existing VM. The current VM must exist. If it has been deleted, you can't use this option. Azure Backup takes a snapshot of the existing VM before replacing the disk, and it stores the snapshot in the staging location that you specify. Existing disks connected to the VM are replaced with the selected restore point. The snapshot is copied to the vault and retained in accordance with the retention policy.  After the replace\-disk operation, the original disk is retained in the resource group. You can choose to manually delete the original disks if they aren't needed. This option is supported for unencrypted managed VMs and for VMs [created from custom images](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/tutorial-custom-images). It's not supported for unmanaged disks and VMs, classic VMs, and [generalized VMs](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/capture-image-resource). If the restore point has more or fewer disks than the current VM, the number of disks in the restore point will only reflect the VM configuration. This option is also supported for VMs with linked resources, like [user\-assigned managed identity](../active-directory/managed-identities-azure-resources/overview) and [Azure Key Vault](/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/overview). |
| **Cross Region (secondary region)** | You can use cross\-region restore to restore Azure VMs in the secondary region, which is an [Azure paired region](/en-us/azure/reliability/cross-region-replication-azure). You can restore all the Azure VMs for the selected recovery point if the backup is done in the secondary region. This feature is available for the following options: \- [Create a VM](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#create-a-vm)  \- [Restore disks](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#restore-disks)  We don't currently support the [Replace existing disks](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#replace-existing-disks) option. Backup admins and app admins have permissions to perform the restore operation on a secondary region. |
| **Cross Subscription** | Allowed only if the [Cross Subscription Restore property](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#cross-subscription-restore-for-azure-vm) is enabled for the required target scenario.  You can restore managed Azure virtual machines or disks to a different subscription within the same tenant by using the following options: \- [Create a VM](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#create-a-vm)  \- [Restore disks](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#restore-disks)  The default target subscription is the protected VM subscription. Snapshot\-tier recovery points can be restored only in the protected VM subscription. Vault\-tier recovery points can be restored in the protected VM subscription or the vault subscription. To restore a vault\-tier recovery point to another subscription, Cross Subscription Restore must be enabled on the vault.  Original location restore and [Replace existing](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#replace-existing-disks) remain supported only in the protected VM subscription.  Cross Subscription Restore is unsupported for:  \- Legacy recovery points from [VMs that used unmanaged disks](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#restore-legacy-recovery-points-from-vms-that-used-unmanaged-disks) and [VMs with disks having Azure Encryptions (ADE)](backup-azure-vms-encryption#encryption-support-by-using-ade).  \- [VMs with CMK encrypted disks](backup-azure-vms-encryption). |
| **Cross Zonal Restore** | You can use cross\-zonal restore to restore Azure zone\-pinned VMs in available zones. You can restore Azure VMs or disks to different zones (one of the Azure RBAC capabilities) from restore points. Note that when you select a zone to restore, it selects the [logical zone](/en-us/azure/reliability/availability-zones-overview#zonal-and-zone-redundant-services) (and not the physical zone) as per the Azure subscription you will use to restore to.  This feature is available for the following options: \- [Create a VM](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#create-a-vm)  \- [Restore disks](backup-azure-arm-restore-vms#restore-disks)  Cross\-zonal restore is unsupported for [snapshots](backup-azure-vms-introduction#snapshot-creation) of restore points.  Cross\-zonal restore doesn't support restoring [encrypted Azure VMs](backup-azure-vms-introduction#encryption-of-azure-vm-backups) directly. If you perform a restore, the restored VM uses **SSE encryption** by default. You must manually reapply **CMK encryption** to the restored VM after the restore process is complete. |
| **Cross Tenant (preview)** | You can restore vaulted recovery points of managed Azure virtual machines to a different tenant by using [cross\-tenant restore](cross-tenant-restore-overview). Only alternate location restore is supported.  Cross\-tenant restore is unsupported for Confidential VMs, VMs encrypted with Azure Disk Encryption (ADE), original location restore, and archive\-tier recovery points. |

answer:
Soft delete in Azure Backup is a feature that retains deleted backup data for a configurable period to enable recovery [11]. Azure Backup provides retention configuration that determines how long soft deleted items are retained before permanent deletion [10].

Retention details:
- For virtual machine backups, deleted backup data is retained in a soft-delete state for 14 days [2].
- For Azure files, deleted file shares and their recovery points (snapshots) are retained for at least 14 days in a soft-deleted state [3][4].
- More generally, soft delete retains deleted backup items for a configured retention period of 14 to 180 days before permanent deletion [1].

Additional behavior: while an item is in the soft-deleted state, Azure Backup retains its recovery points and does not clean them on expiry per the backup policy [9]. Soft-deleted items appear in the Recovery Services vault with a red soft-delete icon during the 14-day retention period [8], and a vault containing soft-deleted items cannot be deleted [7]. Azure Backup also offers Enhanced soft delete, which allows customizing the retention period and making soft delete always-on to protect against being disabled by malicious actors [14].

answer:
To restore a SQL Server database from an Azure Backup vault:

**Permissions required:**
- Backup Operator permissions in the vault where you're doing the restore [1]
- Contributor (write) access to the source VM that's backed up [1]
- Contributor (write) access to the target VM (the source VM if restoring to the same VM, or the new target VM if restoring to an alternate location) [1]

**Steps:**
1. In the Azure portal, go to **Resiliency** and select **Recover** [1]
2. On the **Recover** pane, select **Datasource type** as **SQL in Azure VM**, and under **Protected item**, click **Select** [1]
3. Select a protected SQL database from the list and click **Select** [1]
4. Select **Continue** [1]
5. Under **Where and how to restore**, choose a restore location [1]:
   - **Alternate Location**: restore to an alternate location and keep the original source database [1]
   - **Original Location**: restore to the same SQL Server instance as the original source (overwrites the original database). Note: if the database belongs to an Always On availability group, only Alternate Location is available [1]
   - **Restore as files**: restore the backup files instead of a database, to be recovered later using SQL Server Management Studio [1]

**For alternate location restore:**
- Select the SQL Server name and instance, enter the restored DB name, optionally select overwrite if a DB with the same name exists [3]
- Select a restore point — either point in time (log backups) or a specific full/differential recovery point [3]
- Under Advanced Configuration, you can enable **Restore with NORECOVERY** to keep the database nonoperational, or change target file paths [3]
- Select **OK** to trigger the restore; track progress in Notifications or the Backup Jobs view [3]

**Prerequisites to note:**
- The destination server must be registered to the same vault as the source, and you can restore to a SQL Server instance in the same Azure region [2]
- Point-in-time restore is available only for log backups for databases in full and bulk-logged recovery mode [3]
- For TDE-encrypted databases restored to another SQL Server, first restore the certificate to the destination server [2]
- CDC-enabled databases and the "master" database should be restored using the Restore as files option [2]

**Cross Subscription Restore:** By default, Azure Backup restores to the same subscription where the restore points are available, but with CSR (enabled by default on all Recovery Services vaults) you can restore to any subscription and vault under your tenant, subject to Azure RBAC requirements [10].

citations.text:
Restore SQL Server database from the vault
Restore SQL Server databases on Azure VMs > Restore prerequisites

Restore SQL Server databases on Azure VMs
This article describes how to restore a SQL Server database that's running on an Azure virtual machine (VM) that the [Azure Backup](backup-overview) service has backed up to an Azure Backup Recovery Services vault.

This article describes how to restore SQL Server databases. For more information, see [Back up SQL Server databases on Azure VMs](backup-azure-sql-database).

To view the backup and restore scenarios that we support today, see the [support matrix](sql-support-matrix#scenario-support). For common questions, see the [frequently asked questions](faq-backup-sql-server).

Restore to a time or a recovery point
Azure Backup can restore SQL Server databases that are running on Azure VMs as follows:

* Restore to a specific date or time (to the second) by using transaction log backups. Azure Backup automatically determines the appropriate full differential backup and the chain of log backups that are required to restore based on the selected time.
* Restore a specific full or differential backup to restore to a specific recovery point.

Before you restore a database, note the following:

* You can restore the database to an instance of a SQL Server in the same Azure region.
* The destination server must be registered to the same vault as the source. If you want to restore backups to a different vault, [enable Cross Subscription Restore](#cross-subscription-restore).
* If you have multiple instances running on a server, all the instances should be up and running. Otherwise the server won't appear in the list of destination servers for you to restore the database to. For more information, refer to [the troubleshooting steps](backup-sql-server-azure-troubleshoot#faulty-instance-in-a-vm-with-multiple-sql-server-instances).
* To restore a TDE\-encrypted database to another SQL Server, you need to first [restore the certificate to the destination server](/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/encryption/move-a-tde-protected-database-to-another-sql-server).
* [CDC](/en-us/sql/relational-databases/track-changes/enable-and-disable-change-data-capture-sql-server) enabled databases should be restored using the [Restore as files](#restore-as-files) option.
* We strongly recommended to restore the "master" database using the [Restore as files](#restore-as-files) option and then restore [using T\-SQL commands](/en-us/sql/relational-databases/backup-restore/restore-the-master-database-transact-sql).
* For all system databases (model, msdb), stop the SQL Server Agent service before you trigger the restore.
* Close any applications that might try to take a connection to any of these databases.
* For the **master databases**, the **Alternate Location** option for restore isn't supported. We recommend you to restore the **master database** using the **Restore as files** option, and then restore using the `T-SQL` commands.
* For `msdb` and `model`, the **Alternate Location** option for restore is supported only when the **Restored database name** is different from the **target database** name. If you want to restore the same name with the **target database**, we recommend you to restore using the **Restore as files** option, and then restore using the `T-SQL` commands.

Azure Backup now allows you to restore SQL database to any subscription (as per the following Azure RBAC requirements) from the restore point. By default, Azure Backup restores to the same subscription where the restore points are available.

With Cross Subscription Restore (CSR), you have the flexibility of restoring to any subscription and any vault under your tenant if restore permissions are available. By default, CSR is enabled on all Recovery Services vaults (existing and newly created vaults).

Note

* You can trigger Cross Subscription Restore from Recovery Services vault.
* CSR is supported only for streaming based backup and is not supported for snapshot\-based backup.
* Cross Regional Restore (CRR) with CSR is not supported.

**Azure RBAC requirements**

| Operation type | Backup operator | Recovery Services vault | Alternate operator |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Restore database or restore as files | `Virtual Machine Contributor` | Source VM that got backed up | Instead of a built\-in role, you can consider a custom role which has the following permissions:  \- `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write`  \- `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read` |
|  | `Virtual Machine Contributor` | Target VM in which the database will be restored or files are created. | Instead of a built\-in role, you can consider a custom role that has the following permissions:  \- `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write`  \- `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read` |
|  | `Backup Operator` | Target Recovery Services vault |  |

By default, CSR is enabled on the Recovery Services vault. To update the Recovery Services vault restore settings, go to **Properties** \> **Cross Subscription Restore** and make the required changes.

[

![Screenshot shows how to modify the Cross Subscription Restore settings on a Recovery Services vault for SQL database.](/media/8f869443-b48d-4a45-a9fb-7d0df772e632/4a0bb8a63205.png)

> **Figure:** Screenshot of the 'Properties' page for a Recovery Services vault, showing the 'Cross Subscription Restore' settings dialog with the 'Enable Cross Subscription Restore' option selected.

](media/sap-hana-db-restore/cross-subscription-restore-settings-for-database.png#lightbox)

answer: Azure Backup uses platform-managed keys (PMKs) as the default encryption method for Azure VMs [4]. To use customer-managed keys (CMKs) instead, Azure Backup requires CMKs to encrypt backup data in a Backup vault [1], and the Recovery Services vault also supports using a customer-managed key to encrypt backup data [13]. CMKs used to encrypt backup data must be stored in Azure Key Vault [8], and CMK can be used with system-assigned managed identity [2]; Azure Backup also integrates with UserAssignedIdentities for CMK encryption [6]. Configuring encryption settings requires registering the 'Microsoft.DataProtection' resource provider at the subscription level [10], and Azure Backup provides Encryption Settings [9]. Azure Backup does not decrypt backup data at any point in Azure [7]. Additionally, the MARS agent provides a passphrase to encrypt data before upload and decrypt after download [5], requiring a passphrase of at least 16 characters [14]. Azure Backup also integrates with Microsoft Entra ID for encrypted VMs using BEK and KEK [11] and backs up encrypted Azure VMs [12].

answer:
Configuring Cross Region Restore in Azure Backup is done in the Azure portal: for the Recovery Services vault, navigate to Properties, Backup Configuration, and enable Cross Region Restore [1][4]; the portal is also used to configure Cross Region Restore for the backup vault [2].

Running it: when Cross Region Restore is enabled on the Backup Vault, Azure Backup enables restores in the paired Azure region [6], restoring data in a secondary Azure paired region [14]. When GRS is configured on a vault, Microsoft makes backups in the paired region available after an outage in the primary region occurs [8]. Cross Region Restore (preview) lets you restore backup data from a secondary region [7].

Workload-specific notes: for AKS, it uses a Geo-redundant vault with Cross Region Restore enabled, with copies of backups in the secondary region (Azure Paired region) stored in the Vault Tier to restore AKS clusters when the primary region is unavailable [12]. For Azure Database for PostgreSQL servers, Azure PowerShell is used to configure and perform cross-region restore [10]. System State can be restored from a secondary region if enabled in the vault [11]. For Liberty on AKS, the portal is used to configure and manage Cross Region Restore, including selecting the secondary region for restoring a Kubernetes Services backup instance [13]. The capability is also documented with examples in backup-azure-vms-automation [5], and Azure Backup Vault provides it as an optional capability (--cross-region-restore-state) [15].

Note: Azure Backup does not support cross-region backup and restore in the case where the backup vault and disk must be in the same region [3], and a Backup vault with Cross Region Restore configured is required [9].

answer:
To back up an encrypted Azure VM:

**Before you start:**
- Ensure you have Windows or Linux VMs with Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) enabled [4].
- Create a Recovery Services vault if you don't have one [3][4].
- If you enable encryption on VMs already enabled for backup, provide Azure Backup permissions to access the key vault so backups continue without disruption [4].

**Configure backup:**
1. Go to **Resiliency** and select **+ Configure protection** [3].
2. On the Configure protection pane, set **Resources managed by** to **Azure**, **Datasource type** to **Azure Virtual machines**, and **Solution** to **Azure Backup**, then select **Continue** [3].
3. Select the Recovery Services vault and continue [3].
4. Assign a backup policy — the default policy backs up once a day, retaining backups for 30 days and instant recovery snapshots for 2 days; or create a custom policy [3].
5. Under **Virtual Machines**, select **Add**, choose the encrypted VMs, and select **OK** [3].
6. If using Key Vault, you may see a message that Azure Backup needs read-only access to keys and secrets; if so, set permissions as described in the procedure [3].
7. Select **Enable Backup** to deploy the policy and enable backup for the selected VMs [9].

**Key vault permissions:**
- Azure Backup needs read-only access to back up keys and secrets. Member users get access automatically; guest users must provide permissions [8].
- You can set an access policy using the **Azure Backup** template (removing key permissions if the VM uses BEK only), or use PowerShell/Azure CLI [8].
- For RBAC-enabled key vaults, assign the **Key Vault Administrator** role to the Backup Management Service Microsoft Entra app, or create a custom role with the required data actions [10].

**Trigger a backup:**
The initial backup runs per schedule, but you can run it immediately: go to **Resiliency** > **Protected items**, select **Azure Virtual machines** as the datasource type, find the VM, select **Backup Now**, choose the retention date, and monitor via **Resiliency** > **Jobs** [1].

**Note:** ADE is scheduled for retirement in September 2028; after that, ADE backup is blocked, so consider migrating to encryption at host [6].

Before you start, follow these steps:

Back up and restore encrypted Azure virtual machines > Provide permissions

Azure Backup needs read\-only access to back up the keys and secrets, along with the associated VMs.

* Your key vault is associated with the Microsoft Entra tenant of the Azure subscription. If you're a member user, Azure Backup acquires access to the key vault without further action.
* If you're a guest user, you must provide permissions for Azure Backup to access the key vault. You need to have access to key vaults to configure Azure Backup for encrypted VMs.

To provide Azure RBAC permissions on a key vault, see [Enable RBAC permissions on a key vault](/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/rbac-guide?tabs=azure-cli#enable-azure-rbac-permissions-on-key-vault).

To set permissions:

1. In the Azure portal, select **All services**, and search for **Key vaults**.
2. Select the key vault associated with the encrypted VM that you're backing up.

Tip

To identify a VM's associated key vault, use the following PowerShell command. Substitute your resource group name and VM name:

`Get-AzVm -ResourceGroupName "MyResourceGroup001" -VMName "VM001" -Status`

Look for the key vault name in this line:

`SecretUrl : https://<keyVaultName>.vault.azure.net`
3. Select **Access policies** \> **Add Access Policy**.

4. For **Add access policy** \> **Configure from template (optional)**, select **Azure Backup**.

	* The required permissions are prefilled for **Key permissions** and **Secret permissions**.
	* If your VM is encrypted by using **BEK only**, remove the selection for **Key permissions** because you need permissions only for secrets.

It shows the 'Enable Access to' options with 'Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption' selected, and a list of current access policies for an application and a user, including their permissions and delete actions.

Back up and restore encrypted Azure virtual machines

This article describes how to back up and restore Windows or Linux Azure virtual machines (VMs) with encrypted disks by using [Azure Backup](backup-overview). For more information, see [Encryption of Azure VM backups](backup-azure-vms-introduction#encryption-of-azure-vm-backups).

Azure Disk Encryption (ADE) is scheduled for retirement in September 2028\. After this date, ADE backup is blocked and restore operations might not work as expected. Consider migrating existing ADE\-enabled VMs to encryption at host. For the latest retirement timeline and migration guidance, see the official [ADE overview](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/disk-encryption-overview) and [Migrate from Azure Disk Encryption to encryption at host](/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/disk-encryption-migrate) documentation.

Supported scenarios for backup and restore of encrypted Azure VMs
This section describes the supported scenarios for backup and restore of encrypted Azure VMs.

To restore a SQL Server database from an Azure Backup vault, you need Backup Operator permissions in the vault where you're doing the restore [3], and the destination server must be registered to the same vault as the source [8].

Azure Backup provides several restore options:

- **Restore as files**: Azure Backup provides the RestoreAsFiles capability to restore a SQL DB as.bak files [11]. The backup files can then be restored as a database using SQL Server Management Studio on any machine where the files are present [2][4].
- **Point-in-time and overwrite restore**: Azure Backup supports restoring SQL Server databases from a vault, including restore as files, point-in-time restore, and overwrite restore [1].
- **Restore to another instance**: Azure Backup supports restoring SQL Server databases as a new DB in another SQL instance in another SQL VM (AlternateWorkloadRestore) [9], and can restore the database to an instance of SQL Server in the same Azure region [5].
- **Azure CLI**: Azure Backup supports restoring SQL databases using the Azure CLI with workload-type SQLDataBase [6], and provides the `az backup restore restore-azurewl` command to restore a database using a recovery config object [12].
- **Azure portal**: You can restore tenant databases by going to the Restore pane, selecting Tenant database(s), selecting the target VM, selecting the restore point, validating, and selecting OK to restore [10]. Similarly, you can restore the system database by going to the Restore pane, selecting System Database (Including attach and mount), selecting the target VM, selecting the restore point, validating, and selecting OK [14].

For the master database specifically, Azure Backup recommends restoring it using the Restore as files option, and then restoring using T-SQL commands [7].

answer:
To change the retention period, edit your backup plan: open the AWS Backup console, choose **Backup plans**, select the plan, select the backup rule, change the retention setting, and save [3]. Changes to a backup plan only affect backups created in the future; existing backups keep their original retention period [3]. For continuous backups, you must use the backup plan to change retention (you cannot use `UpdateRecoveryPointLifecycle`), and the change takes effect when the next backup completes [2].

Service-specific behavior:
- Amazon S3: changing retention makes the recovery point `STOPPED` and a new continuous recovery point is created with the new settings [6].
- Aurora/RDS and SAP HANA on EC2: the existing recovery point is updated rather than a new one being created [6].
- Amazon RDS PITR: AWS Backup calls `ModifyDBInstance` to apply the change; non-zero to non-zero changes apply immediately, while first-time enablement and disabling are scheduled for the next maintenance window [10].

You can also edit the lifecycle of an individual backup (transition to cold storage and expiration) via Backup vaults → choose the backup → Edit [4]. Note that backups transitioned to cold storage must remain there at least 90 days, so retention must be 90 days greater than the "transition to cold after days" setting [1][4].

citations.text:
Update a backup plan

After creating a backup plan, you can edit the plan—for example, you can add tags,
 or you can add, edit, or delete backup rules. Any changes that you make to a backup plan have
 no effect on existing backups created by the backup plan. The changes apply only to backups
 that are created in the future. 

For example, when you update the retention period in a backup rule, the retention period
 of backups created before you made the update remain the same. Any backups that are created by
 that rule going forward reflect the updated retention period.

To edit a backup plan using the AWS Backup console
1. Open the AWS Backup console at <https://console.aws.amazon.com/backup>.
2. In the navigation pane, choose **Backup plans**.
3. Under the second pane, **Backup plans**, existing back plans are
 displayed. Select the underlined link in the column **Backup plan name**
 to see details of the chosen backup plan.
4. You can edit a backup rule, view resource assignments, view backup jobs, manage tags,
 or change Windows VSS settings.
5. To update a backup rule, select the name of the backup rule.

Select **Manage tags** to add or delete tags.

Select **Edit** next to **Advanced backup settings**
